findings.title: Traffic recorded today could be decrypted later by a quantum computer
findings.detail: The session keys come from secp256r1 alone. Shor’s algorithm recovers the private value behind the public key share sent in the handshake, so an attacker who stores this traffic can decrypt it once a large enough quantum computer exists ("harvest now, decrypt later"). No such computer exists today. This is the most urgent quantum risk because the recording can happen now.

learn.label: Watch a recorded session being decrypted

findings.title: Certificate key: RSA 2048-bit
findings.detail: Issued to localhost by "CN=pq-oidc lab issuing CA (rsa)", valid until 2026-12-31. The server sent 2 certificates.

evidence.label: Leaf
evidence.value: CN=tls12.lab.localhost; key RSA 2048-bit; signed by "CN=pq-oidc lab issuing CA (rsa)" with RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256

evidence.label: Chain #1
evidence.value: CN=pq-oidc lab issuing CA (rsa); key RSA 2048-bit; signed by "CN=pq-oidc lab root (rsa)" with RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256

findings.title: The server proved it holds that key with rsa_pss_rsae_sha256
findings.detail: The scanner checked ServerKeyExchange, a signature over the key-exchange parameters against the leaf certificate’s public key. It is valid.

findings.title: The certificate chain is not trusted: the issuing certificate authority is not in the trust store
findings.detail: Checked by OpenSSL against the CA certificates shipped with Node.js v25.9.0 (Mozilla’s list). Expected for a lab server: its certificate authority exists only on this machine.

findings.title: A quantum computer could impersonate this server, but only at the time of an attack
findings.detail: The server’s identity rests on the certificate key (RSA 2048-bit) and a chain signature (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256). Shor’s algorithm recovers such private keys from the public keys, which would let an attacker present this identity. Unlike key exchange, this cannot be used on recorded traffic: the forgery has to be made, with a working quantum computer, during a live connection while the certificate is still valid. Publicly trusted certificate authorities do not issue post-quantum certificates yet, so a public site cannot change this alone today.

findings.title: Data is encrypted with AES-128-GCM
findings.detail: Cipher suite TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. The key for it comes out of the key exchange above; the cipher itself uses no public-key cryptography.

findings.title: A 128-bit key keeps a reduced margin against a quantum computer
findings.detail: Quantum computers do not break symmetric ciphers. Grover’s algorithm could in theory search a 128-bit key in about 2^64 steps, but the steps cannot be spread across machines the way a classical search can, and NIST treats AES-128 as its baseline security category. Guidance that plans decades ahead, such as CNSA 2.0, asks for AES-256.

findings.title: No HSTS header
findings.detail: Without Strict-Transport-Security a browser will use plain HTTP if a link or an attacker sends it there.

findings.title: Cookie session can be sent over plain HTTP
findings.detail: A cookie without the Secure attribute is sent on plain-HTTP requests too, where anyone on the network path can read it. Whether that matters depends on what the cookie is for, which a scan cannot tell: for a session cookie it means the session can be stolen.

evidence.label: session
evidence.value: not Secure, readable by scripts, no SameSite

findings.title: An attacker on the network can keep a first-time visitor off HTTPS
findings.detail: With no HSTS, a browser that is sent to the plain-HTTP address makes that request in the clear. An attacker on the path can answer it and never let the TLS handshake happen. The strength of the key exchange is irrelevant to a connection that was never encrypted. This is a classical attack, not a quantum one.

findings.title: Unable to determine the application-level token signing algorithm
findings.detail: No OpenID Connect or OAuth metadata is published at this address. A service can issue signed tokens without saying how; from outside that is only visible in a token itself. If this system gives you a token, paste it into the token analyzer.

learn.label: Analyze a token from this system

findings.title: Internal dependencies cannot be observed from outside
findings.detail: Connections between your own services, databases, key storage, vendor APIs and the devices your users connect from all use cryptography too. None of it is visible to an external scan. Finding it is the first step of a migration.
